questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Eigenvalues of a 3x3 Matrix Containing a Block of Zeros
questions.problem:
Find the characteristic equation of the matrix 
$B=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 3 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ -3 & 5 & 1\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the matrix $\,B-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
B-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -4 & 3 \\ 0 & -2-\lambda  & 0 \\ -3 & 5 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}]
$$

The characteristic equation is $det(B-\lambda I)=0.$ 

Expanding the determinant across the $2$nd row, we obtain the following:  

$$
\begin{aligned}det(B-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -4 & 3 \\ 0 & -2-\lambda  & 0 \\ -3 & 5 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-2-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 3 \\ -3 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-2-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-(3)(-3)) & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +10) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Determine all real eigenvalues $\lambda $ of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ -5 & 3 & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 6\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the matrix $\,A-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & 0 & 0 \\ -5 & 3-\lambda  & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 6-\lambda \end{aligned}]
$$

The characteristic equation is $det(A-\lambda I)=0.$ 

Since the determinant of a triangular (or diagonal) matrix is given by the product of the entries on the main diagonal, we obtain the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & 0 & 0 \\ -5 & 3-\lambda  & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 6-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )(3-\lambda )(6-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (\lambda -4)(\lambda -3)(\lambda -6) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ $\,{\lambda }_{2}=4,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=6.$

**Note:** The eigenvalues of a triangular (or diagonal) matrix are always the entries on the main diagonal.

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Eigenvalues of a 4x4 Matrix Containing a Block of Zeros
questions.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 & -6 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 7 \\ 0 & -3 & -4 & 9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Consider the matrix $P$ given above. Which of the following statements are true?

- $\lambda =0$ is an eigenvalue of $P$
- $\lambda =-4$ is an eigenvalue of $P$
- The eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ has algebraic multiplicity $2$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the matrix $\,P-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
P-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & 2 & -6 & 8 \\ 0 & -\lambda  & 0 & 7 \\ 0 & -3 & -4-\lambda  & 9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}]
$$

The characteristic equation is $det(P-\lambda I)=0.$ 

Notice that we can expand the $4\times 4$ determinant across the $1$st column, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(P-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & 2 & -6 & 8 \\ 0 & -\lambda  & 0 & 7 \\ 0 & -3 & -4-\lambda  & 9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}-\lambda  & 0 & 7 \\ -3 & -4-\lambda  & 9 \\ 0 & 0 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, expanding the $3\times 3$ determinant across the $3$rd row, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}(5-\lambda )\cdot (2-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}-\lambda  & 0 \\ -3 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )(2-\lambda )(-\lambda )(-4-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (\lambda -5)(\lambda -2)\lambda (\lambda +4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $P$ are $\lambda =5,$ $\lambda =2,$ $\lambda =0,$ and $\lambda =-4$  (all with algebraic multiplicity $1$).

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -9 & -18 & -3 \\ 0 & -10 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -10 & 0 \\ -18 & 18 & -36 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

Consider the matrix $P$ given above. Which of the following statements are true?

- $\lambda =-1$ is an eigenvalue of $P$
- $\lambda =-10$ is an eigenvalue of $P$
- The eigenvalue $\lambda =-10$ has algebraic multiplicity $3$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the matrix $\,P-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
P-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & -9 & -18 & -3 \\ 0 & -10-\lambda  & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -10-\lambda  & 0 \\ -18 & 18 & -36 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}]
$$

The characteristic equation is $det(P-\lambda I)=0.$ 

Notice that we can expand the $4\times 4$ determinant across the $2$nd row, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(P-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & -9 & -18 & -3 \\ 0 & -10-\lambda  & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -10-\lambda  & 0 \\ -18 & 18 & -36 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-10-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & -18 & -3 \\ 0 & -10-\lambda  & 0 \\ -18 & -36 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, expanding the $3\times 3$ determinant across the $2$nd row, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-10-\lambda )\cdot (-10-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & -3 \\ -18 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-10-\lambda )^{2}((-1-\lambda )(-4-\lambda )-54) & =0 \\ (\lambda +10)^{2}({\lambda }^{2}+5\lambda -50) & =0 \\ (\lambda +10)^{2}(\lambda +10)(\lambda -5) & =0 \\ (\lambda +10)^{3}(\lambda -5) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $P$ are $\lambda =-10$ (with algebraic multiplicity $3$) and $\lambda =5.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

﻿﻿﻿

questions.problem:
Determine all real eigenvalues $\lambda $ of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the matrix $\,A-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}]
$$

The characteristic equation is given by $det(A-\lambda I)=0.$ 

Expanding the determinant across the $1$st row, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 3 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}|-1|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-{\lambda }^{3}+6\lambda +5)-(-1-\lambda ) & =0 \\ -{\lambda }^{3}+7\lambda +6 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{3}-7\lambda -6 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to solve this equation. We find the first root by testing some values. According to the rational zeros theorem, a list of good first guesses consists of all divisors of $6:$ 

$$
\pm 1,\pm 2,\pm 3,\pm 6
$$

- Let's pick $x=1.$ Substituting to the characteristic equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(1)^{3}-7(1)-6 & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lambda =1$ is not a root of the equation.

- Let's pick $x=-1.$ Substituting to the characteristic equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)^{3}-7(-1)-6 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lambda =-1$ is a root of the equation.

So, we can factor $(\lambda +1)$ out of ${\lambda }^{3}-7\lambda -6$ using synthetic division:

| $-1$ | $1$ | $0$ | $-7$ | $-6$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $↓$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $6$ |
|  | $1$ | $-1$ | $-6$ | $0$ |

So, we obtain the following factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda +1)({\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -6) & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)(\lambda +2)(\lambda -3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=3.$

questions.problem:
Determine all real eigenvalues $\lambda $ of the matrix 
$O=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the matrix $\,O-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
O-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -\lambda \end{aligned}]
$$

The characteristic equation is given by $det(O-\lambda I)=0.$ 

Expanding the determinant across the $1$st row, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(O-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & -\lambda \end{aligned}|+1|\begin{aligned}0 & -1-\lambda  \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-{\lambda }^{3}-2{\lambda }^{2}+1)+(\lambda +1) & =0 \\ -{\lambda }^{3}-2{\lambda }^{2}+\lambda +2 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{3}+2{\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to solve this equation. We find the first root by testing some values. According to the rational zeros theorem, a list of good first guesses consists of all divisors of $2:$ 

$$
\pm 1,\pm 2
$$

Let's pick $x=1.$ Substituting to the characteristic equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(1)^{3}+2(1)^{2}-(1)-2 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lambda =1$ is a root of the equation. So, we can factor $(\lambda -1)$ out of ${\lambda }^{3}+2{\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -2$ using synthetic division:

| $1$ | $1$ | $2$ | $-1$ | $-2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $↓$ | $1$ | $3$ | $2$ |
|  | $1$ | $3$ | $2$ | $0$ |

So, we obtain the following factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda -1)({\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda +2) & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +2)(\lambda +1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=-1.$

\begin{aligned}(3-\lambda )\cdot (4-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 5 \\ 7 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )(4-\lambda )((-1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-35) & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )(4-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-36) & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)(\lambda -4)(\lambda -6)(\lambda +6) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $P$ are $\lambda=3,$ $\lambda=4,$ $\lambda=6,$ and $\lambda=-6$ (all with algebraic multiplicity $1$).

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."
